THOUGHT: Young sexually active female with inconsistent condom use presenting with 5 days of lower abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, dysuria and recent dyspareunia. Exam shows fever (38.5°C), purulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness — classic findings of upper genital tract infection. Marked inflammatory response with leukocytosis (15,000) and very elevated ESR (100) supports an acute infectious/inflammatory process. These features meet CDC clinical criteria for pelvic inflammatory disease (lower abdominal pain plus cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness and evidence of cervicitis). Differential would include complicated PID such as salpingitis or tubo-ovarian abscess (imaging not yet done), acute cervicitis/urethritis, urinary tract infection, appendicitis, or ectopic pregnancy (pregnancy test not reported and must be obtained). The most likely diagnosis given purulent discharge, CMT, fever, leukocytosis, and sexual history is acute PID — most commonly due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis (gonococcal infection particularly likely with purulent discharge and severe presentation). Further workup should include pregnancy test, NAAT for GC/CT, and pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for tubo-ovarian abscess; treatment for PID should be initiated promptly per guidelines.
DIAGNOSIS: Acute pelvic inflammatory disease (acute salpingitis/PID), most likely gonococcal or chlamydial in etiology.
